column3: A strike at school; other strikes have their own words, such as 罷工 for workers and 罷市 for shopkeepers.
column4: 学生们为了抗议学费上涨而罢课。
column5: 學生們為了抗議學費上漲而罷課。
column6: Xuéshengmen wèile kàngyì xuéfèi shàngzhǎng ér bàkè.
column7: The students went on strike to protest the rise in tuition.

column3: A saying for after you have seen something yourself, or to urge someone to come and see it; it is used as a complete remark on its own.
column4: 百闻不如一见，你亲自来看看吧。
column5: 百聞不如一見，你親自來看看吧。
column6: Bǎiwénbùrúyījiàn, nǐ qīn zì lái kàn kan ba.
column7: Seeing is believing; come and see for yourself.

column3: It usually means the building where an organization, such as a school, factory or government body, keeps its offices. A room is placed by its floor: 三樓.
column6: Xiàozhǎngshì zài bàngōnglóu sān lóu.
column7: The principal's office is on the third floor of the administration building.

column3: Doubling makes 抱 warm and child-like: it is what you say to a child, a pet or a loved one, often as an invitation (來，抱抱) or as comfort. A plain 抱 is neutral.
column6: Lái, ràng māma bàobào nǐ.
column7: Come here, let Mommy give you a hug.

column3: The everyday word for a runny nose in Taiwan, nearly always with 流: 流鼻水. On the mainland people say 鼻涕: 流鼻涕.
column6: Tā gǎnmào le, yīzhí liú bíshuǐ.
column7: He has a cold and his nose keeps running.

column3: Its opposite is 選修課, an elective. The verb for taking a course is 修, as in 修必修課.
column4: 这学期我要修三门必修课。
column5: 這學期我要修三門必修課。
column6: Zhè xuéqī wǒ yào xiū sān mén bìxiūkè.
column7: This semester I have to take three required courses.

column3: Nearly always with 搭: 搭便車 is to catch a ride with someone already going that way. The same phrase is used for being a free rider on other people's effort.
column6: Wǒ dā tóngshì de biànchē huí jiā.
column7: I got a ride home with a coworker.

column3: The full name of the convenience store; in Taiwan people often shorten it to 超商, while the mainland says 便利店.
column6: Wǒ qù biànlìshāngdiàn mǎi kāfēi.
column7: I'm going to the convenience store to buy coffee.

column3: A lofty word for love that reaches everyone alike, not just family and friends. In Taiwan 博愛座 is the priority seat on buses and the MRT.
column4: 他的博爱精神让大家很敬佩。
column5: 他的博愛精神讓大家很敬佩。
column6: Tā de bó'ài jīngshén ràng dàjiā hěn jìngpèi.
column7: His spirit of universal love earns everyone's respect.

column3: The seats on Taiwan's buses and MRT trains kept for the elderly, pregnant women, people with disabilities and others who need them, marked with signs. The name comes from 博愛, loving everyone; on the mainland they are 愛心專座.
column6: Qǐng bǎ bó'àizuò ràng gěi lǎorén.
column7: Please give the priority seat to the elderly.

column3: It opens a sentence the way English says "anyway": whatever the situation, the point after the comma still holds, often with 還是 or 都, as in 不管怎樣，我還是要去。
column4: 不管怎样，我都会支持你。
column5: 不管怎樣，我都會支持你。
column6: Bùguǎnzěnyàng, wǒ dōu huì zhīchí nǐ.
column7: No matter what, I will support you.

column3: Before a verb it often means unpleasant or hard to do: 不好吃 (doesn't taste good), 不好找 (hard to find). It also starts the apology 不好意思. 不 began as a picture of the calyx of a flower.
column6: Zhè jiā cāntīng de cài bùhǎo chī.
column7: The food at this restaurant doesn't taste good.

column3: It takes a noun after it: 不合口味 (not to one's taste), 不合規定 (against the rules), 不合時宜 (out of step with the times).
column6: Zhè dào cài bùhé wǒ de kǒuwèi.
column7: This dish is not to my taste.

column3: A polite reply to 謝謝, though 不客氣 is the more common answer; in Taiwan a casual 不會 is also heard.
column6: Bùxiè, zhè shì wǒ yīnggāi zuò de.
column7: You're welcome, it is what I should do.

column3: The ordinary kitchen knife, with the measure word 把: 一把菜刀. It is usually a broad blade used for most of the cutting in a kitchen.
column6: Qǐng bǎ càidāo fàng zài zhēnbǎn shàng.
column7: Please put the kitchen knife on the cutting board.

column3: A news-style image of a queue snaking along like a dragon, almost always with 排: 排成長龍 or 大排長龍.
column4: 这家店很有名，门口每天都排起长龙。
column5: 這家店很有名，門口每天都排起長龍。
column6: Zhè jiā diàn hěn yǒumíng, ménkǒu měitiān dōu pái qǐ chánglóng.
column7: This shop is famous; a long line forms at its door every day.

column3: Set against 小孩 and 未成年人. It appears in rules and warnings (成年人才可以購買), and in the sense of someone who should know better: 成年人要為自己負責.
column4: 成年人要为自己的选择负责。
column5: 成年人要為自己的選擇負責。
column6: Chéngniánrén yào wèi zìjǐ de xuǎnzé fùzé.
column7: Adults must take responsibility for their own choices.

column3: The 飽 is a result added to 吃: 吃飽了 "have eaten enough", 吃不飽 "can't get full". In Taiwan, 吃飽沒? is also a friendly greeting, much like "how are you?", not a real question about food. The character 吃 was made for the word "to stutter", and "to eat" may originally have been written 喫.
column6: Wǒ chībǎo le, xièxie.
column7: I'm full, thank you.

column3: The 不 in the middle makes it "can't", and the positive form is 吃得下. The same pattern works with other verbs: 坐不下 means there is no room to sit, 裝不下 that it won't fit in.
column4: 我已经饱了，真的吃不下了。
column5: 我已經飽了，真的吃不下了。
column6: Wǒ yǐjīng bǎo le, zhēn de chībuxià le.
column7: I am already full; I really can't eat any more.

column3: The usual Taiwan word for all-you-can-eat, seen on restaurant signs; the same pattern gives 喝到飽 for drinks. On the mainland a buffet is usually 自助餐.
column4: 这家火锅店是吃到饱,一个人只要五百元。
column5: 這家火鍋店是吃到飽,一個人只要五百元。
column6: Zhè jiā huǒguō diàn shì chīdàobǎo, yī gè rén zhǐ yào wǔ bǎi yuán.
column7: This hot pot place is all-you-can-eat, only 500 dollars a person.

column3: A verb plus its object, so other words can slip between them: 抽了兩管血 (drew two tubes of blood), 抽過血 (has had blood drawn).
column4: 明天早上要空腹去医院抽血。
column5: 明天早上要空腹去醫院抽血。
column6: Míngtiān zǎoshang yào kōngfù qù yīyuàn chōuxuè.
column7: Tomorrow morning I have to go to the hospital on an empty stomach to have blood drawn.

column3: Fermented tofu, fried or steamed, sold at street stalls and night markets. Its name is a joke people repeat: it smells bad (臭) but tastes good (香).
column4: 臭豆腐闻起来很臭，吃起来却很香。
column5: 臭豆腐聞起來很臭，吃起來卻很香。
column6: Chòudòufu wén qǐlái hěn chòu, chī qǐlái què hěn xiāng.
column7: Stinky tofu smells bad but tastes delicious.

column3: Said of fishermen and boats leaving the harbor: 出海捕魚 means going out fishing. The business sense of expanding abroad is a recent usage in mainland tech and trade news, as in 企業出海.
column6: Yúmín tiān yī liàng jiù chūhǎi le.
column7: The fishermen went out to sea as soon as it got light.

column3: A river in names and set phrases (四川, 山川, 川流不息); in speech a river is 河. It is a written, slightly literary word.
column6: Jiē shang de chēliàng chuān liú bù xī.
column7: Vehicles stream along the street without a break.

column3: Formal and a little old-fashioned: obeying an order or giving in to a request from someone above you, such as an elder. It is best known from the set phrase 恭敬不如從命.
column4: 长辈既然这么说，我只好从命。
column5: 長輩既然這麼說，我只好從命。
column6: Zhǎngbèi jìrán zhème shuō, wǒ zhǐhǎo cóngmìng.
column7: Since my elder puts it that way, I have no choice but to do as asked.

column3: It goes before the verb and says the activity fills the whole day, so it often sounds like a complaint about being busy or tired. The pattern 從…到… marks a start and an end, so other pairs fit too: 從頭到尾, 從南到北.
column4: 他从早到晚都在写报告。
column5: 他從早到晚都在寫報告。
column6: Tā cóngzǎodàowǎn dōu zài xiě bàogào.
column7: He is writing reports from morning to night.

column3: Used for the very largest cities, in speech and in the news: an ordinary 城市 is a city, a 大都市 is on the scale of Shanghai or Tokyo.
column4: 上海是一座国际大都市。
column5: 上海是一座國際大都市。
column6: Shànghǎi shì yī zuò guójì dàdūshì.
column7: Shanghai is an international metropolis.

column3: A unit inside a larger organization: soldiers, police and fire crews are grouped into 大隊, with smaller 中隊 below. It can also mean a big crowd moving together, as in 大隊人馬.
column6: Dàduì rénmǎ yǐjīng dào le.
column7: The whole main force has already arrived.

column3: Said of an experience, trip or show that shows you something new; the usual frame is 讓 someone 大開眼界, or 大開了眼界 for your own.
column4: 这次去日本玩，真的让我大开眼界。
column5: 這次去日本玩，真的讓我大開眼界。
column6: Zhè cì qù Rìběn wán, zhēn de ràng wǒ dàkāiyǎnjiè.
column7: This trip to Japan really opened my eyes.

column3: Said when someone gets the chance to show what they can do, often with 終於 or 有機會; it is praise or eager anticipation.
column4: 这次比赛,他终于有机会大显身手了。
column5: 這次比賽,他終於有機會大顯身手了。
column6: Zhè cì bǐsài, tā zhōngyú yǒu jīhuì dàxiǎnshēnshǒu le.
column7: At this match he finally gets the chance to show what he can do.

column3: Two meanings: an odd number in math (1, 3, 5), also called 奇數, and singular in grammar. The matching words are 雙數 for an even number and 複數 for plural.
column4: 他家的门牌号码是单数。
column5: 他家的門牌號碼是單數。
column6: Tā jiā de ménpái hàomǎ shì dānshù.
column7: His house number is an odd number.

column3: The general term for knives and blades as tools, in a kitchen, a workshop or a shop; it appears in rules such as 管制刀具, regulated knives.
column6: Chúfáng lǐ de dāojù yào fàng hǎo.
column7: Put the kitchen knives away properly.

column3: The 德 is short for 德國 (the country), and the same pattern gives 英文 and 日文; 德語 is an equally common name for the spoken language.
column6: Wǒ zhèngzài xué Déwén.
column7: I'm learning German.

column3: What you say to ask someone to hold on. The 一下 softens it: a bare 等 sounds like an order. Before a verb it means "in a moment" or "later", as in 我等一下再打給你.
column6: Děngyīxià, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
column7: Wait a moment, I'll be right there.

column3: It is a verb plus its object, so it splits: 點了三道菜 means ordered three dishes. For ordering a meal at a counter or on a screen, 點餐 is also common.
column6: Wǒmen kěyǐ diǎncài le ma?
column7: May we order now?

column3: Used for choosing something on a screen by tapping or clicking it, so its object is typically a menu item, a link or an option.
column6: Qǐng diǎnxuǎn nǐ xiǎng yào de xuǎnxiàng.
column7: Please click the option you want.

column3: It follows a number to give the hour: 三點鐘. In speech people often say just 三點, and 鐘 is dropped once minutes are added (三點十分).
column6: Xiànzài shì sān diǎnzhōng.
column7: It is three o'clock now.

column3: Electricity as a supply or resource, in phrases such as 電力公司 (power company), 電力供應 and 電力不足 (a shortage).
column4: 台风过后，这个地区的电力还没恢复。
column5: 颱風過後，這個地區的電力還沒恢復。
column6: Táifēng guòhòu, zhè ge dìqū de diànlì hái méi huīfù.
column7: After the typhoon, power in this area has not yet been restored.

column3: The usual word in Taiwan, as in 電玩店 or 打電玩. On the mainland people say 電子遊戲 or just 遊戲.
column6: Tā zhōumò dōu zài jiā dǎ diànwán.
column7: He plays video games at home every weekend.

column3: Gambling as an activity or a vice, often in a warning or a legal context: 賭博成癮, 非法賭博. A single friendly bet is 打賭.
column4: 在这个国家，赌博是违法的。
column5: 在這個國家，賭博是違法的。
column6: Zài zhè ge guójiā, dǔbó shì wéifǎ de.
column7: Gambling is illegal in this country.

column3: It covers a marching column, an army and any organized group: 遊行隊伍 is a parade, 志願者隊伍 a team of volunteers. A sports team is usually 球隊, and waiting in line is 排隊.
column4: 游行的队伍走过了街道。
column5: 遊行的隊伍走過了街道。
column6: Yóuxíng de duìwǔ zǒu guò le jiēdào.
column7: The parade went down the street.

column3: Asks about age, size or extent. For a person your own age or younger, 你今年多大? is natural; to an older person it sounds blunt, so ask 您今年多大年紀?
column6: Nǐ jīnnián duōdà?
column7: How old are you this year?

column3: It describes things you could do without: 多餘的話 are needless words, 多餘的步驟 an unnecessary step. Said of a person, it means someone is not needed or in the way.
column6: Zhè jù huà shì duōyú de.
column7: This sentence is unnecessary.

column3: The 俄 is short for 俄羅斯 (Russia), as 英 and 法 are in 英文 and 法文.
column6: Tā huì shuō Éwén.
column7: He can speak Russian.

column3: It names how power is made, usually after the source: 風力發電 is wind power, 水力發電 hydropower, and a power plant is a 發電廠.
column6: Fēnglì fādiàn yuè lái yuè pǔbiàn.
column7: Wind power is becoming more and more common.

column3: Used for real madness, but far more often as an exaggeration: 快發瘋了 (about to go crazy) over noise, stress or a long wait; it can also mean throwing a fit.
column4: 等了三个小时,我都快发疯了。
column5: 等了三個小時,我都快發瘋了。
column6: Děng le sān gè xiǎoshí, wǒ dōu kuài fāfēng le.
column7: After waiting three hours I am about to go crazy.

column3: The 法 is short for 法國 (France), and 文 names the language, as in 英文 and 日文. It is the usual word for French, spoken or written; 法語 names the same language and is a bit more formal or about speech.
column6: Tā huì shuō Fǎwén.
column7: She can speak French.

column3: Mostly seen in news and notices about going back home for a holiday or after years away, as in 返鄉過年 or 返鄉潮. In speech people say 回老家 on the mainland and more often 回家 or 回鄉下 in Taiwan.
column6: Tā měi nián guònián dōu huì fǎnxiāng.
column7: He goes back to his home town every New Year.

column3: A set phrase for keeping a routine whatever happens. It comes before the verb, often with 地, as in 風雨無阻地送報, or it closes a promise: every day, rain or shine.
column4: 他每天早上风雨无阻地去公园跑步。
column5: 他每天早上風雨無阻地去公園跑步。
column6: Tā měitiān zǎoshang fēngyǔwúzǔ de qù gōngyuán pǎobù.
column7: Every morning, rain or shine, he goes jogging in the park.

column3: In Taiwan this is the usual word for a restaurant server, where the mainland says 服務員. The 生 is an ending for a person in a trade, as in 學生 and 實習生.
column6: Fúwùshēng, wǒmen yào diǎncān.
column7: Waiter, we'd like to order.

column3: The standard word for waiters and waitresses on the mainland, and you can call it out to get their attention: 服務員！ It also covers hotel and shop attendants. The ending 員 names a person by work, as in 店員 and 公務員.
column6: Fúwùyuán, qǐng gěi wǒ càidān.
column7: Waiter, please give me the menu.

column3: It describes the bad side of something and almost always comes before a noun: 負面新聞, 負面影響, 負面情緒. The opposite is 正面.
column4: 这件事给他带来了负面影响。
column5: 這件事給他帶來了負面影響。
column6: Zhè jiàn shì gěi tā dàilái le fùmiàn yǐngxiǎng.
column7: This brought him a negative impact.

column3: The everyday way to say you pay at a shop or restaurant. 付 also takes an amount or a bill (付五百塊, 付房租); the formal word is 付款.
column6: Wǒ lái fùqián, nǐmen xiān zuò.
column7: I will pay; you all sit down first.

column3: Today it mostly means confessing romantic feelings, with the person introduced by 向 or 對: 向她告白. The sense of a public announcement is old-fashioned.
column6: Tā zuótiān xiàng tā gàobái le.
column7: Yesterday he confessed his feelings to her.

column3: A polite set phrase for accepting an offer or invitation. A host or elder insists, and you stop declining and give in, with some humor.
column4: 既然您这么热情，那我就恭敬不如从命了。
column5: 既然您這麼熱情，那我就恭敬不如從命了。
column6: Jìrán nín zhème rèqíng, nà wǒ jiù gōngjìngbùrúcóngmìng le.
column7: Since you are so kind about it, I will gladly accept.

column3: Beijing's Forbidden City, and also the National Palace Museum in Taipei, which people just call 故宮. Which one is meant depends on where you are.
column6: Wǒmen míngtiān qù gùgōng.
column7: We're going to the Palace Museum tomorrow.

column3: For looking at something pleasing at leisure: flowers, scenery, fish, a performance. As a modifier it means ornamental, as in 观赏鱼 and 观赏植物.
column4: 春天很多人去山上观赏樱花。
column5: 春天很多人去山上觀賞櫻花。
column6: Chūntiān hěn duō rén qù shān shàng guānshǎng yīnghuā.
column7: In spring many people go up the mountain to enjoy the cherry blossoms.

column3: In speech a turtle or tortoise is usually 烏龜, with 海龜 for a sea turtle; 龜 on its own turns up in set phrases and as a name. It began as a drawing of a turtle seen from the side and from above.
column4: 你听过龟兔赛跑的故事吗？
column5: 你聽過龜兔賽跑的故事嗎？
column6: Nǐ tīngguo guī tù sàipǎo de gùshi ma?
column7: Have you heard the story of the tortoise and the hare?

column3: The line between two countries; 邊界 also covers borders between regions. It lives on in sayings like 科學沒有國界 and in 無國界醫生, Doctors Without Borders.
column6: Kēxué méiyǒu guójiè.
column7: Science has no borders.

column3: A scholar in the field is a 漢學家, and a department abroad is often a 漢學系.
column6: Tā zài dàxué lǐ yánjiū Hànxué.
column7: He studies Chinese studies at the university.

column3: It names the direction of a dictionary, translation or course: 漢英詞典 goes from Chinese to English, and 英漢詞典 is the reverse.
column6: Wǒ mǎi le yī běn hànyīng cídiǎn.
column7: I bought a Chinese-English dictionary.

column3: It is added to the end of a suggestion or request to ask for agreement, and makes it softer than a plain order. Answer with 好 or 不好.
column4: 我们明天去看电影，好不好？
column5: 我們明天去看電影，好不好？
column6: Wǒmen míngtiān qù kàn diànyǐng, hǎobuhǎo?
column7: Let's go to a movie tomorrow, okay?

column3: The partner of 好吃, which is for food. The same 好 + verb pattern makes 好看, 好聽 and 好用.
column6: Zhè bēi chá hěn hǎohē.
column7: This cup of tea is really good.

column3: You say it of things you can do or try, such as a game, a trip or a place. For something interesting to think about rather than to do, 有意思 fits better.
column6: Zhège yóuxì hěn hǎowán.
column7: This game is a lot of fun.

column3: It is the fall colors as a sight people travel to see: 賞紅葉 means going leaf-viewing. A maple leaf in particular is 楓葉. 紅 first meant a lighter red, and gradually took over from 赤 as the basic word for red.
column4: 秋天到了，山上的红叶很美。
column5: 秋天到了，山上的紅葉很美。
column6: Qiūtiān dào le, shān shàng de hóngyè hěn měi.
column7: Autumn has come and the red leaves on the mountain are beautiful.

column3: Mostly seen in the titles of magazines heavy on photos and pictures; for a magazine in general, the everyday word is 雜誌.
column6: Tā xǐhuan kàn lǚyóu huàbào.
column7: He likes reading travel picture magazines.

column3: For a regular train station; the high-speed rail has its own, 高鐵站, and a subway station is 捷運站 in Taiwan but 地鐵站 on the mainland.
column6: Qǐngwèn, huǒchēzhàn zěnme zǒu?
column7: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?

column3: It comes before a verb to say someone is in a hurry to do it, and is often negative or a question: 別急著下結論 (don't jump to conclusions), 急著用錢 (needing money in a hurry).
column6: Nǐ bié jízhe zǒu, zài zuò yī xià.
column7: Don't be in a hurry to leave; sit a bit longer.

column3: Asks for a clock time only, and the answer uses 點: 三點, 五點半. For a date ask 幾號, for how long ask 多久. In simplified writing 幾 shares its shape 几 with a separate character, one meaning a small table.
column6: Nǐ jǐdiǎn qǐchuáng?
column7: What time do you get up?

column3: A verb plus a result: what fills the space comes after, usually with 了, as in 擠滿了人 (packed with people).
column6: Zhōumò de yèshì jǐmǎn le rén.
column7: The night market is packed with people at the weekend.

column3: As a noun it is a taboo, often about luck, such as what not to say at a wedding; as a verb, 犯忌諱 means to break one.
column4: 这件事在我们家是个忌讳。
column5: 這件事在我們家是個忌諱。
column6: Zhè jiàn shì zài wǒmen jiā shì ge jìhuì.
column7: This matter is taboo in our family.

column3: What you buy or keep to remember a trip or an event, and often bring home for friends; the usual verb is 買 or 送.
column4: 我在机场买了一些纪念品送朋友。
column5: 我在機場買了一些紀念品送朋友。
column6: Wǒ zài jīchǎng mǎi le yīxiē jìniànpǐn sòng péngyou.
column7: I bought some souvenirs at the airport to give to friends.

column3: The ending 器 turns an action into the device that does it: 計算 is to calculate, 計算器 the calculator, as 充電 and 充電器 (charger).
column4: 考试的时候可以用计算器吗？
column5: 考試的時候可以用計算器嗎？
column6: Kǎoshì de shíhou kěyǐ yòng jìsuànqì ma?
column7: May I use a calculator during the exam?

column3: A woman whose work is running the home, with 家庭主夫 as the word for a man. A mother at home with young children may also be called 全職媽媽.
column4: 她结婚后成了家庭主妇。
column5: 她結婚後成了家庭主婦。
column6: Tā jiéhūn hòu chéng le jiātíngzhǔfù.
column7: After marrying she became a housewife.

column3: Describes a person or a scheme that is crafty and cannot be trusted, always as criticism; typical in 為人奸詐 and 奸詐小人. It sounds written or literary rather than casual.
column6: Nàge shāngrén hěn jiānzhà.
column7: That merchant is very crafty.

column3: A noun for the short blurb about a book, company, person or product, placed before the full details, as in 作者简介 and 内容简介.
column4: 请先看一下这本书的简介。
column5: 請先看一下這本書的簡介。
column6: Qǐng xiān kàn yīxià zhè běn shū de jiǎnjiè.
column7: Please read this book's summary first.

column3: A short, newsy phrase for cutting carbon emissions. In Taiwan the slogan is 節能減碳 (save energy, cut carbon); on the mainland the set phrase is usually 节能减排.
column4: 我们每个人都可以为减碳出一份力。
column5: 我們每個人都可以為減碳出一份力。
column6: Wǒmen měi ge rén dōu kěyǐ wèi jiǎntàn chū yī fèn lì.
column7: Each of us can do our part to cut carbon.

column3: These are the sheets a teacher prepares and hands out for a course, not the textbook itself; the usual verbs are 發 (hand out) and 印 (print).
column6: Lǎoshī fā le jīntiān de jiǎngyì.
column7: The teacher handed out today's handout.

column3: A somewhat formal, written word, found in films, novels and news. In everyday speech people say 親 or 親親 instead.
column6: Tāmen zài diànyǐng lǐ jiēwěn.
column7: They kiss in the movie.

column3: It works as a verb and as an adjective before a thing: 節能燈泡 is an energy-saving bulb, and appliances are advertised as 節能. In Taiwan policy the set phrase is 節能減碳; on the mainland it is usually 节能减排.
column4: 这台冷气很节能，电费不高。
column5: 這台冷氣很節能，電費不高。
column6: Zhè tái lěngqì hěn jiénéng, diànfèi bù gāo.
column7: This air conditioner saves energy, so the electric bill is not high.

column3: An idiom for winning something by being the first to act, such as a job, a bargain or a good seat. It is often heard after someone has lost out: 被別人捷足先登了.
column4: 那间房子被别人捷足先登了。
column5: 那間房子被別人捷足先登了。
column6: Nà jiān fángzi bèi biérén jiézúxiāndēng le.
column7: Somebody else got to that house first.

column3: A formal word for breaking a bad habit or addiction, as in 戒除菸癮 or 戒除惡習; for everyday talk about smoking, people just say 戒菸. 戒 shows hands holding up a weapon as a warning.
column4: 他终于戒除了抽烟的习惯。
column5: 他終於戒除了抽菸的習慣。
column6: Tā zhōngyú jièchú le chōuyān de xíguàn.
column7: He finally gave up the habit of smoking.

column3: A short, slightly written form for the morning of today, common in news (今早發生…); in ordinary speech people say 今天早上.
column6: Wǒ jīnzǎo méi chī zǎocān.
column7: I did not eat breakfast this morning.

column3: Said from the viewpoint of someone out in the countryside or on the edge of town, heading in for shopping, a doctor or work; the opposite is 出城.
column6: Wǒ míngtiān yào jìnchéng mǎi dōngxi.
column7: Tomorrow I am going into town to shop.

column3: The place where a road, corridor or tunnel runs out, or figuratively where hope, patience or a life runs out. It most often follows a noun with 的, as in 路的盡頭, and is common after 走到, as in 走到人生的盡頭.
column4: 这条路的尽头有一家咖啡店。
column5: 這條路的盡頭有一家咖啡店。
column6: Zhè tiáo lù de jìntóu yǒu yī jiā kāfēidiàn.
column7: There is a coffee shop at the end of this road.

column3: The police as an organization, mostly in news reports: 警方表示, 警方調查. For one officer you say 警察, never 警方.
column4: 警方正在调查这起事件。
column5: 警方正在調查這起事件。
column6: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ shìjiàn.
column7: The police are investigating this incident.

column3: It suits a small, old-style place that serves wine and food, like a tavern in a story; for a modern bar or pub, 酒吧 is the common word.
column6: Wǒmen qù jiǔguǎn hē yī bēi ba.
column7: Let's go have a drink at the tavern.

column3: Used when people come together in one place for a meal, a talk or an event, so the subject is normally several people.
column4: 过年的时候，全家人都聚在一起吃饭。
column5: 過年的時候，全家人都聚在一起吃飯。
column6: Guò nián de shíhou, quán jiā rén dōu jùzàiyīqǐ chī fàn.
column7: At New Year the whole family gets together to eat.

column3: A place to sit and drink coffee. 館 names a place of service, as in 圖書館; 咖啡廳 and 咖啡店 are also common, especially in Taiwan. 啡 is used in loanwords for its sound alone, and 咖啡 is a loanword.
column6: Wǒmen zài kāfēiguǎn jiànmiàn ba.
column7: Let's meet at a café.

column3: The everyday way to say reading a book, for pleasure or for study; 讀書 leans toward studying.
column6: Wǒ zhōumò xǐhuan zài jiā kànshū.
column7: On weekends I like to read at home.

column3: The usual Taiwan word for a university department or field of study, as in 選科系 (choosing a major); on the mainland you hear 院系 or 專業.
column6: Nǐ xiǎng dú shénme kēxì?
column7: Which department do you want to study in?

column3: 家 after a field names an expert in it, as in 音樂家 and 作家; many ordinary jobs end in 員 or 師 instead, as 公務員 and 教師.
column4: 这位科学家研究海洋生物。
column5: 這位科學家研究海洋生物。
column6: Zhè wèi kēxuéjiā yánjiū hǎiyáng shēngwù.
column7: This scientist studies marine life.

column3: The standard phrase in news and weather reports, often with 嚴重 (serious) or 改善 (improve), and in 空氣污染指數 for the air pollution index.
column4: 空气污染在冬天特别严重。
column5: 空氣污染在冬天特別嚴重。
column6: Kōngqìwūrǎn zài dōngtiān tèbié yánzhòng.
column7: Air pollution is especially bad in winter.

column3: A written word for something running dry: rivers, wells and resources (資源枯竭), and figuratively inspiration or funds (靈感枯竭).
column4: 这口井的水已经枯竭了。
column5: 這口井的水已經枯竭了。
column6: Zhè kǒu jǐng de shuǐ yǐjīng kūjié le.
column7: The water in this well has dried up.

column3: Describes a room, house, car or street with plenty of space. It does not give a measured width: for that, use 寬, as in 這條河很寬.
column6: Zhè jiān kètīng yòu dà yòu kuānchang.
column7: This living room is big and roomy.

column3: Said of someone with years of experience at a job or craft; the opposite is 新手, a beginner.
column6: Tā shì xiū chē de lǎoshǒu.
column7: He is an old hand at fixing cars.

column3: Rarely used alone for a forest: in speech you say 森林 or 樹林. Alone it is mostly the common surname Lin, as in 林先生, or part of a name.
column6: Lín xiānsheng shì wǒ de lǎoshī.
column7: Mr. Lin is my teacher.

column3: In modern speech it is only a surname, one of the most common: 我姓劉, 劉老師, and 小劉, a friendly way to address a younger person named Liu.
column6: Wǒ xìng Liú, qǐng duōduō zhǐjiào.
column7: My surname is Liu; please look after me.

column3: 七 and 八 are not counting anything; they only pile on emphasis. It is very common after 弄, 搞 or 得, as in 弄得亂七八糟, and it can describe a room, a plan or a state of mind.
column6: Tā de fángjiān luànqībāzāo.
column7: His room is a complete mess.

column3: It means shopping for the household's food, at a market or store, and is what you say about the daily errand: 去買菜. It is not used for buying other things.
column4: 妈妈每天早上去市场买菜。
column5: 媽媽每天早上去市場買菜。
column6: Māma měitiān zǎoshang qù shìchǎng mǎicài.
column7: Mom goes to the market to buy groceries every morning.

column3: On its own it is mostly a word for the grain in general; in daily life you meet it in compounds such as 小麥, 大麥, 燕麥 and 麥片. 來, now the word for "to come", was originally the character for wheat.
column6: Wǒ měi tiān zǎoshang dōu chī mài piàn.
column7: I eat oat cereal every morning.

column3: It is a stock reply when something can't be helped, often followed by what you do instead. Before a verb it means there is no way you can: 我今天沒辦法去.
column6: Méibànfǎ, jīntiān zhǐ néng jiābān.
column7: Nothing to be done; today I have to work overtime.

column3: Colloquial for something gone or used up: 錢沒了 means the money is gone. It can also be a plain way to say a person has died.
column6: Qián dōu méile, zěnme bàn?
column7: The money is all gone. What do we do?

column3: The everyday answer to a request: "Can you help me?" "沒問題." It also states plainly that nothing is wrong, and the fuller 沒有問題 means the same.
column4: 你能帮我拿一下吗？没问题。
column5: 你能幫我拿一下嗎？沒問題。
column6: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ ná yīxià ma? Méiwèntí.
column7: Can you hold this for me for a moment? No problem.

column3: You say it of a movie, game or talk that fails to interest you, and also of a plan that has no point. Its opposite, 有意思, means interesting or fun.
column6: Zhè bù diànyǐng zhēn méiyìsi.
column7: This movie is really boring.

column3: Hair-thin noodles; the Taiwan style is cooked soft in a thick broth, as in 蚵仔麵線, with oysters. Because the noodle is so long, it is eaten on birthdays for long life.
column4: 我想吃一碗热热的面线。
column5: 我想吃一碗熱熱的麵線。
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chī yī wǎn rè rè de miànxiàn.
column7: I would like a bowl of hot misua.

column3: You write it (寫明信片) and send it (寄明信片). Literally an "open" letter card, one that travels without an envelope.
column4: 我从台北寄了一张明信片给你。
column5: 我從台北寄了一張明信片給你。
column6: Wǒ cóng Táiběi jì le yī zhāng míngxìnpiàn gěi nǐ.
column7: I sent you a postcard from Taipei.

column3: What staff in Taiwan ask when you order food: 內用還是外帶? The mainland word for eating in is 堂食. As a term for medicine, 內用 means taken by mouth, the opposite of 外用.
column6: Qǐngwèn nèiyòng háishi wàidài?
column7: Eating in or taking out?

column3: Fine for a first greeting or with a stranger; for someone you should show respect, 您好, and for a group, 大家好. Close friends often skip it and just start talking.
column4: 你好，请问洗手间在哪里？
column5: 你好，請問洗手間在哪裡？
column6: Nǐhǎo, qǐngwèn xǐshǒujiān zài nǎlǐ?
column7: Hello, excuse me, where is the restroom?

column3: Young people as a group, or a young person, usually seen from outside, as when older people talk about 现在的年轻人.
column4: 现在的年轻人都喜欢用手机。
column5: 現在的年輕人都喜歡用手機。
column6: Xiànzài de niánqīngrén dōu xǐhuan yòng shǒujī.
column7: Young people today all like using their phones.

column3: The meat only, never the animal (that is 牛). It heads many food words such as 牛肉麵 and 牛肉乾, and it is bought by weight: 一斤牛肉.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chī niúròu miàn.
column7: I want to eat beef noodles.

column3: The everyday word for a girl, with 男孩 for a boy, and often 小女孩 for a young one. The measure word is 個. 孩 alone is not used on its own: it only turns up in words such as 小孩 and 孩子.
column4: 那个小女孩在公园里玩。
column5: 那個小女孩在公園裡玩。
column6: Nà ge xiǎo nǚhái zài gōngyuán lǐ wán.
column7: That little girl is playing in the park.

column3: A lofting, tossing throw, as in 拋硬幣 (flip a coin) or 拋球; the everyday word for throw is 扔 on the mainland and 丟 in Taiwan. It also appears in 拋棄 (abandon).
column6: Tā bǎ yìngbì pāo xiàng kōngzhōng.
column7: He tossed the coin into the air.

column3: Used both for people (abandoning a family, dumping a partner) and for ideas or things (giving up a plan or an old way of thinking); with people it sounds hurtful.
column4: 他不肯抛弃自己的家人。
column5: 他不肯拋棄自己的家人。
column6: Tā bù kěn pāoqì zìjǐ de jiārén.
column7: He refuses to abandon his own family.

column3: 泡 is steeping something in hot water, so the same verb gives 泡咖啡 and 泡麵; pouring tea into a cup is 倒茶.
column4: 爷爷每天早上都会泡茶。
column5: 爺爺每天早上都會泡茶。
column6: Yéye měitiān zǎoshang dōu huì pàochá.
column7: Grandpa makes tea every morning.

column3: In Taiwan, 騎士 is the everyday word for the rider of a scooter or bicycle, as in 機車騎士 in traffic news and rules. Everywhere it also means a knight, which gives 騎士精神, chivalry.
column4: 机车骑士一定要戴安全帽。
column5: 機車騎士一定要戴安全帽。
column6: Jīchē qíshì yīdìng yào dài ānquánmào.
column7: Scooter riders must wear a helmet.

column3: It is nearly always part of a compound: 汽車 (car), 汽油 (gasoline), 汽水 (soda), 蒸汽 (steam). On its own it is rare.
column6: Tā hē le yī píng qì shuǐ.
column7: He drank a bottle of soda.

column3: Used as a verb for couples holding hands. In Taiwan it can also be a noun for one's spouse, an affectionate word from Taiwanese Hokkien, heard more in songs and from older people than in everyday talk.
column6: Tāmen qiānshǒu zǒu zài hǎibiān.
column7: They walk along the shore holding hands.

column3: A full-price ticket, as against the half-price ones for children or students; in a vote it means unanimous approval.
column4: 大人要买全票，小孩半价。
column5: 大人要買全票，小孩半價。
column6: Dàrén yào mǎi quánpiào, xiǎohái bànjià.
column7: Adults need a full-price ticket; children pay half.

column3: In Taiwan, food labels sort vegetarian food into levels, and 全素 is the strictest: no eggs or dairy, and also none of the five pungent plants such as onion and garlic (unlike 植物五辛素, which allows them). On the mainland the usual word for vegan is 纯素.
column4: 这道菜是全素的,没有蛋也没有奶。
column5: 這道菜是全素的,沒有蛋也沒有奶。
column6: Zhè dào cài shì quánsù de, méiyǒu dàn yě méiyǒu nǎi.
column7: This dish is fully vegan, with no eggs and no dairy.

column3: Named by how it heats: 電熱水器 electric, 太陽能熱水器 solar. The ending 器 names a device, as in 充電器 and 吸塵器.
column6: Wǒ jiā de rèshuǐqì huài le.
column7: The water heater at my house is broken.

column3: What a newcomer says of a place where they know nobody and nothing, often when asking for help: 剛搬來，人生地不熟，請多關照. The 生 here is the 'unfamiliar' of 陌生, the opposite of 熟: the people and the land are both strange.
column4: 我刚搬来，人生地不熟，请多关照。
column5: 我剛搬來，人生地不熟，請多關照。
column6: Wǒ gāng bān lái, rénshēngdìbùshú, qǐng duō guānzhào.
column7: I just moved here and I don't know anyone or anything, so please look after me.

column3: It means agreeing with a view or feeling that a group or value is yours: 我不認同你的看法 (I don't agree with you), 文化認同 (cultural identity), 認同感 (a sense of belonging).
column6: Wǒ bù rèntóng zhè zhǒng zuòfǎ.
column7: I don't agree with this way of doing it.

column3: Used for the sight or the time of day more than for the act: 看日落, 日落前. As a plain statement about the sun, people usually say 太陽下山.
column6: Wǒmen qù hǎibiān kàn rìluò ba.
column7: Let us go to the beach to watch the sunset.

column3: The usual word for Japanese, spoken or written: a 日文 class, a 日文 menu. 日語 names the same language and is a bit more formal or about speech, and 文 makes 英文 and 法文 the same way.
column6: Wǒ zài xué Rìwén.
column7: I am learning Japanese.

column3: A written, slightly formal "if" that opens the clause, like the everyday 如果; the main clause often follows with 就 or 那麼.
column4: 若是明天下雨,我们就改天再去。
column5: 若是明天下雨,我們就改天再去。
column6: Ruòshì míngtiān xià yǔ, wǒmen jiù gǎitiān zài qù.
column7: If it rains tomorrow, we will go another day.

column3: The formal word for a funeral; you attend it (參加) or hold it (舉行). Here 喪 is read sāng; read sàng, it means to lose something abstract but important.
column6: Tāmen zài jiàotáng jǔxíng sānglǐ.
column7: They are holding the funeral in the church.

column3: It names the people, not the act: 上班 is going to work. The ending 族 makes a social group, as in 月光族 or 追星族. 上班族 means employees on fixed hours, with a hint of daily routine.
column4: 早上的车站挤满了上班族。
column5: 早上的車站擠滿了上班族。
column6: Zǎoshang de chēzhàn jǐ mǎn le shàngbānzú.
column7: In the morning the station is packed with office workers.

column3: Said alone, it can also hint at sex, so for plain bedtime people usually add 睡覺: 上床睡覺.
column4: 我今天很累，想早点上床睡觉。
column5: 我今天很累，想早點上床睡覺。
column6: Wǒ jīntiān hěn lèi, xiǎng zǎo diǎn shàngchuáng shuìjiào.
column7: I'm very tired today and want to go to bed early.

column3: The thing you are hooked on follows 對, as in 對遊戲上癮, and it can be said half in jest of food, shows or any habit that pulls you back.
column6: Tā duì shǒujī yóuxì shàngyǐn le.
column7: He has become addicted to mobile games.

column3: About physical skill shown in action, as in 身手不凡 (remarkable skill) and 身手敏捷 (nimble), not book knowledge.
column4: 这位年轻的消防员身手很敏捷。
column5: 這位年輕的消防員身手很敏捷。
column6: Zhè wèi niánqīng de xiāofángyuán shēnshǒu hěn mǐnjié.
column7: This young firefighter is very agile.

column3: A set greeting, said to the person on the day or sent in a message, often as 祝你生日快樂. The same 快樂 pattern works for other occasions: 新年快樂, 聖誕快樂. 樂 is read lè in this word, meaning happy; read yuè it means music.
column4: 大家一起唱歌，祝她生日快乐。
column5: 大家一起唱歌，祝她生日快樂。
column6: Dàjiā yī qǐ chànggē, zhù tā shēngrìkuàilè.
column7: Everyone sang together and wished her a happy birthday.

column3: A polite apology for a small impropriety, such as interrupting someone or taking a call; it can also describe rude behavior.
column6: Shīlǐ le, wǒ xiān jiē ge diànhuà.
column7: Excuse me, let me take a call first.

column3: A full, firm "yes, that's right" confirming what someone said; in casual talk people more often answer 對 or just 嗯.
column6: Shìde, wǒ shì zhèlǐ de xuésheng.
column7: Yes, I am a student here.

column3: Used before a noun, as in 室內運動 and 室內設計, and as a place after 在, as in 在室內; the opposite is 室外.
column4: 外面下雨,我们改在室内活动。
column5: 外面下雨,我們改在室內活動。
column6: Wàimiàn xià yǔ, wǒmen gǎi zài shìnèi huódòng.
column7: It is raining outside, so we are moving the activity indoors.

column3: A verb said twice, then 看, softens a suggestion into "try it and see", and the pattern works with many verbs: 吃吃看, 問問看, 聽聽看.
column4: 你要不要试试看这件衣服？
column5: 你要不要試試看這件衣服？
column6: Nǐ yào bu yào shìshikàn zhè jiàn yīfu?
column7: Do you want to try this piece of clothing on?

column3: Common in cooking, storage and science: 放到室溫 means let it come to room temperature, and 室溫下保存 means keep at room temperature.
column4: 鸡蛋要先放到室温再用。
column5: 雞蛋要先放到室溫再用。
column6: Jīdàn yào xiān fàng dào shìwēn zài yòng.
column7: Let the eggs come to room temperature before you use them.

column3: A radio is a 收音機, named for this word. 收音 itself is picking up a signal or, in recording, capturing sound, so a microphone can 收音很好.
column4: 这支麦克风收音很清楚。
column5: 這支麥克風收音很清楚。
column6: Zhè zhī màikèfēng shōuyīn hěn qīngchu.
column7: This microphone picks up sound very clearly.

column3: Means an even number (2, 4, 6); the formal math term is 偶數, with 奇數 for odd. It pairs with 單數 in everyday talk, as with even and odd seats or house numbers.
column6: Shuāngshù de zuòwèi zài zuǒbiān.
column7: The even-numbered seats are on the left.

column3: Rarely used alone in speech, where 想 is the everyday "think". It lives inside words (思考, 思想, 意思, 思念) and set phrases such as 三思而後行.
column4: 他做事总是三思而后行。
column5: 他做事總是三思而後行。
column6: Tā zuò shì zǒngshì sān sī ér hòu xíng.
column7: He always thinks carefully before he acts.

column3: Seen in dates of the old calendar, such as 乙巳年, and in the double-hour 巳時. Learners mix it up with 已 and 己: here the loop is closed all the way, and 己 is open.
column4: 巳时是上午九点到十一点。
column5: 巳時是上午九點到十一點。
column6: Sì shí shì shàngwǔ jiǔ diǎn dào shíyī diǎn.
column7: The hour of the snake is nine to eleven in the morning.

column3: Used with the person: 為父親送終 means being at your father's side at the end. It is a duty and an honor that falls to the family.
column4: 他回到家乡，为父亲送终。
column5: 他回到家鄉，為父親送終。
column6: Tā huí dào jiāxiāng, wèi fùqīn sòngzhōng.
column7: He returned to his hometown to be with his father at the end.

column3: Typical of computers and the internet, as in 搜尋引擎 and 搜尋結果; on the mainland the usual word for this is 搜索.
column4: 我在网络上搜寻这家餐厅的评价。
column5: 我在網路上搜尋這家餐廳的評價。
column6: Wǒ zài wǎngluò shàng sōuxún zhè jiā cāntīng de píngjià.
column7: I searched online for reviews of this restaurant.

column3: A spoken cry of delight or relief at good news. The 太…了 frame also says too much (太貴了, too expensive), but with something good it just stresses how good.
column6: Jīntiān bùyòng shàngbān, tàihǎole!
column7: I don't have to work today, great!

column3: It also works as 'solar' before a thing: 太陽能板 is a solar panel and 太陽能熱水器 a solar water heater.
column6: Wū dǐng shàng zhuāng le tàiyángnéng bǎn.
column7: Solar panels were installed on the roof.

column3: Besides a student sitting through a lesson, it is used for a teacher or visitor sitting in on someone else's class to observe it. 聽 first combined an ear with mouth(s), meaning to listen.
column6: Nǐ jīntiān xiàwǔ qù tīngkè ma?
column7: Are you going to the lecture this afternoon?

column3: A language-class word: two characters or words that sound alike are 同音, and a character that shares a sound with another is a 同音字.
column6: Zhè liǎng ge zì tóngyīn.
column7: These two characters sound the same.

column3: The doubled form of 痛快 is lively and spoken; it is an adverb for doing something fully, without holding back, as in 痛痛快快地玩 or 痛痛快快地哭一場.
column4: 考完试,我们痛痛快快地玩了一天。
column5: 考完試,我們痛痛快快地玩了一天。
column6: Kǎo wán shì, wǒmen tòngtongkuàikuài de wán le yī tiān.
column7: After the exam we played to our hearts' content for a day.

column3: Describes feeling dizzy and unable to see clearly from exhaustion, hunger, illness or too much reading or screen time.
column4: 连续工作十个小时，我已经头昏眼花了。
column5: 連續工作十個小時，我已經頭昏眼花了。
column6: Liánxù gōngzuò shí gè xiǎoshí, wǒ yǐjīng tóuhūnyǎnhuā le.
column7: After ten hours of work in a row, I am dizzy and cannot see straight.

column3: What you say when ordering food to go, the opposite of eating in: at counters it pairs with 內用 in Taiwan and with 堂食 on the mainland. 帶 began as a picture of a woven belt.
column6: Wǒ yào yī ge hànbǎo, wàidài.
column7: I'd like a hamburger, to go.

column3: A good-wish saying for the New Year, a birthday, a new job or a new shop, spoken or written on a card or red banner, often paired with 身體健康. 如意 alone is also a ruyi scepter, a lucky charm.
column4: 新年到了，祝你万事如意。
column5: 新年到了，祝你萬事如意。
column6: Xīnnián dào le, zhù nǐ wànshìrúyì.
column7: The New Year is here; may everything go as you wish.

column3: In daily life it mostly means the waves that heat food: 微波爐 is the oven, and 微波一下 is to zap something. The sense of a ripple on water is literary.
column4: 把饭放进微波炉加热一下。
column5: 把飯放進微波爐加熱一下。
column6: Bǎ fàn fàng jìn wēibō lú jiārè yīxià.
column7: Put the rice in the microwave and heat it up.

column3: Describes a person, place or thing known far and wide. Common frames are 以…闻名 (famous for…) and 闻名世界 or 闻名中外.
column6: Zhè jiā diàn yǐ niúròumiàn wénmíng.
column7: This shop is famous for its beef noodles.

column3: The outside top of a building, often followed by 上: 在屋頂上 is "on the roof". For the roof of a car, say 車頂.
column6: Xiǎo māo zài wūdǐng shàng shuìjiào.
column7: The kitten is sleeping on the roof.

column3: Most often an embarrassing mix-up or blunder, as in 鬧烏龍 (to make a blunder); the tea is 烏龍茶. In Taiwan it can also mean udon, usually written 烏龍麵.
column6: Tā nào le yī gè dà wūlóng.
column7: He made a big blunder.

column3: Said of how a person looks or acts: tired, low in spirits, with no energy to join in, often after bad news or a bad night.
column4: 他昨晚没睡好,今天看起来无精打彩的。
column5: 他昨晚沒睡好,今天看起來無精打彩的。
column6: Tā zuówǎn méi shuì hǎo, jīntiān kàn qǐlái wújīngdǎcǎi de.
column7: He did not sleep well last night and looks listless today.

column3: Describes a device with no cable: 無線網路 (Wi-Fi), 無線耳機; the opposite is 有線. 無線電 is radio communication or a two-way radio; a set for listening is a 收音機. 無 began as a picture of a person dancing with ox tails in both hands to pray for rain; it was then borrowed for "have no", and 舞 took over the dance.
column6: Zhè fù wúxiàn ěrjī hěn hǎoyòng.
column7: These wireless earbuds work well.

column3: Said of things that come in a bewildering range, such as goods, methods or opinions, usually with a hint of being a jumble.
column4: 市场上的手机五花八门,不知道该选哪一个。
column5: 市場上的手機五花八門,不知道該選哪一個。
column6: Shìchǎng shàng de shǒujī wǔhuābāmén, bù zhīdào gāi xuǎn nǎ yī gè.
column7: The phones on the market are of every kind, and I do not know which one to pick.

column3: A party with dancing, from a school dance to a formal ball. A casual party without dancing is 派對 or 聚會.
column6: Zhōumò wǒmen qù cānjiā wǔhuì.
column7: This weekend we're going to a dance.

column3: Language names end in 文 or 語: 文 leans toward the written language and the school subject, 語 toward speaking, and 西班牙語 is just as common.
column6: Wǒ zhèng zài xué Xībānyáwén.
column7: I am studying Spanish.

column3: The year count of the Christian era as said in Taiwan; the mainland says 公元. Taiwan also counts years from 1912, the founding of the Republic, as 民國 years.
column6: Tā zài xīyuán èr líng líng líng nián chūshēng.
column7: He was born in the year 2000.

column3: The customs of a people, place or festival, as in 節日習俗; it describes shared practice, not one person's habit (that is 習慣).
column6: Chūnjié yǒu hěn duō xísú.
column7: The Spring Festival has many customs.

column3: Four feelings that stand for the whole range of emotions; typical frames are 表露喜怒哀乐 (show them) and 不露喜怒哀乐 (hide them).
column4: 他从不在别人面前表露喜怒哀乐。
column5: 他從不在別人面前表露喜怒哀樂。
column6: Tā cóng bù zài biérén miànqián biǎolù xǐnù'āilè.
column7: He never shows his feelings in front of others.

column3: The 個 can be left out (下星期), and 下週 is the shorter, more written form. The same pattern gives 上個星期 for last week.
column6: Xiàgèxīngqī wǒ yào qù Táiběi.
column7: Next week I'm going to Taipei.

column3: A written, old-fashioned word, found in set phrases such as 賢妻良母 (a virtuous wife and good mother) and 聖賢, and in the polite 賢弟 for a younger man.
column6: Tā shì ge xián qī liáng mǔ.
column7: She is a virtuous wife and good mother.

column3: Said of two things that are alike in age, price, meaning or size, as in 年齡相近 and 意思相近. Here 相 is read xiāng, as in “each other”; read xiàng, it means appearance.
column4: 这两个字的意思很相近。
column5: 這兩個字的意思很相近。
column6: Zhè liǎng ge zì de yìsi hěn xiāngjìn.
column7: These two characters are close in meaning.

column3: It has hot soup inside: bite a small hole and sip the soup first, then eat the rest. It comes in a basket, so the measure word is 籠: 一籠小籠包.
column6: Wǒmen diǎn le yī lóng xiǎolóngbāo.
column7: We ordered a basket of soup dumplings.

column3: The idea behind many puns and lucky or unlucky associations: 八 is liked because it is a 諧音 of 發 (get rich), and 四 is avoided because of 死.
column6: Bā shì fā de xiéyīn.
column7: Eight sounds like 'fa' (to get rich).

column3: It means putting characters down by hand, as in a child's handwriting practice. For a letter or an article, say 寫信 or 寫文章. 字 once meant to give birth to and to nurture, a sense that has essentially become obsolete.
column6: Wǒ měi tiān huā bàn xiǎoshí xiězì.
column7: I spend half an hour every day writing characters.

column3: Describes how you feel right now, and often how to calm someone: 別心急. A well-known saying warns that a hasty heart ruins things: 心急吃不了熱豆腐.
column6: Nǐ bié xīnjí, mànmàn lái.
column7: Don't be impatient; take it slowly.

column3: A verb plus its object, so other words can slip in between: 修了兩天的車. The place that does it is a 修車廠.
column4: 我的车坏了，要送去修车。
column5: 我的車壞了，要送去修車。
column6: Wǒ de chē huài le, yào sòng qù xiūchē.
column7: My car broke down, so it has to go in for repair.

column3: A path or line follows it: 沿著河邊走 (walk along the river), 沿著這條路直走; the 著 here is the particle zhe.
column6: Wǒmen yánzhe hǎibiān mànmàn zǒu.
column7: We walked slowly along the seashore.

column3: Your sight blurs or you see things wrongly, from tiredness or age: 老人眼花 and 看得眼花. The idiom 眼花缭乱 means dazzled by too many things.
column4: 年纪大了，看字有点眼花。
column5: 年紀大了，看字有點眼花。
column6: Niánjì dà le, kàn zì yǒudiǎn yǎnhuā.
column7: I am getting old and my eyes blur when I read.

column3: The usual word in Taiwan for a drugstore, where you buy cold medicine or fill a prescription; on the mainland 药店 is the more common word.
column6: Wǒ yào qù yàojú mǎi gǎnmào yào.
column7: I am going to the pharmacy to buy cold medicine.

column3: Used for working, studying or struggling without a break over a long stretch; it praises effort, and sounds a little formal or written.
column4: 他夜以继日地工作,终于完成了论文。
column5: 他夜以繼日地工作,終於完成了論文。
column6: Tā yèyǐjìrì de gōngzuò, zhōngyú wánchéng le lùnwén.
column7: He worked day and night and finally finished his thesis.

column3: One blow cuts it in two: the usual picture for ending a relationship, a link or a bad habit for good, with no going back. It is usually the verb of 和…一刀兩斷.
column4: 他决定和过去一刀两断。
column5: 他決定和過去一刀兩斷。
column6: Tā juédìng hé guòqù yīdāoliǎngduàn.
column7: He decided to make a clean break with the past.

column3: Said of a person, 很有辦法 is praise: someone who always finds a way. Before a verb it means able to manage that: 有辦法解決. A variant of 法, 灋, was written with water and a mythical creature that can distinguish right from wrong.
column4: 他很有办法，什么问题都能解决。
column5: 他很有辦法，什麼問題都能解決。
column6: Tā hěn yǒubànfǎ, shénme wèntí dōu néng jiějué.
column7: He is very resourceful and can solve any problem.

column3: 有線 "wired" pairs with 無線 "wireless": 有線電視 against 無線電視 (broadcast through the air), and likewise 有線網路 and 無線網路.
column4: 我们家装了有线电视，可以看很多台。
column5: 我們家裝了有線電視，可以看很多台。
column6: Wǒmen jiā zhuāng le yǒuxiàndiànshì, kěyǐ kàn hěn duō tái.
column7: We had cable TV installed at home, so we can watch many channels.

column3: It is counted with 把: 一把雨傘. You hold one up with 撐 or 打, and 帶傘 is to bring one along.
column4: 外面下雨，你带雨伞了吗？
column5: 外面下雨，你帶雨傘了嗎？
column6: Wàimiàn xià yǔ, nǐ dài yǔsǎn le ma?
column7: It's raining outside; did you bring an umbrella?

column3: What you say when you have just learned the reason for something that puzzled you; 原來 here carries the sense of "so it turns out".
column4: 原来如此，难怪他今天没来。
column5: 原來如此，難怪他今天沒來。
column6: Yuánláirúcǐ, nánguài tā jīntiān méi lái.
column7: I see, no wonder he didn't come today.

column3: It is counted with 支: 一支圓珠筆. In Taiwan the everyday word is 原子筆; 圓珠筆 is the mainland term and is understood there too. Inside the frame of 圓 sits the old ideogram for a circle, 〇, which became the 口 of 員.
column6: Qǐng jiè wǒ yī zhī yuánzhūbǐ.
column7: Please lend me a ballpoint pen.

column3: An exclamation for the moment you realize something has gone wrong, such as a forgotten key or a missed bus. 糟糕 is the fuller everyday word and fits the same spots. The rice 米 in 糟 perhaps refers to rice wine, and the character first meant “unfiltered”, said of liquor and wine.
column6: Zāole, wǒ wàng le dài yàoshi!
column7: Oh no, I forgot to bring my key!

column3: A morning greeting. Many people just say 早, and on the mainland 早上好 is the usual fuller form, while 早安 is warm and common in Taiwan. At night the matching greeting is 晚安.
column6: Zǎo'ān! Nǐ shuì de hǎo ma?
column7: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

column3: You say it to someone who looks upset, hurt or odd: 你怎麼了? Unlike 怎麼樣 (how is it?), it asks what has gone wrong. About an event it means "what happened?". 怎 is thought to be a contraction of 作 and a word for "what", literally "to do what".
column4: 你怎么了？看起来不太高兴。
column5: 你怎麼了？看起來不太高興。
column6: Nǐ zěnmele? Kàn qǐlái bù tài gāoxìng.
column7: What's wrong? You don't look very happy.

column3: Here 幾 means "a few", not "how many". The tense comes from the sentence, so it can mean the past few days or the next few days.
column6: Zhèjǐtiān wǒ dōu hěn máng.
column7: I have been very busy these past few days.

column3: A drink that began in Taiwan, where people often shorten it to 珍奶. At a shop you also choose the sugar and ice, for example 半糖少冰 (half sugar, less ice). 珍 first meant a rich, robust gemstone, and only later “rare”.
column4: 我想要一杯珍珠奶茶,半糖少冰。
column5: 我想要一杯珍珠奶茶,半糖少冰。
column6: Wǒ xiǎng yào yī bēi zhēnzhūnǎichá, bàn táng shǎo bīng.
column7: I would like a bubble tea, half sugar, less ice.

column3: The last stop on a bus, train or metro line, the one announced on board; the first stop is 起點站. It is also used loosely for the final stop of a journey or of life.
column4: 这班公车的终点站是火车站。
column5: 這班公車的終點站是火車站。
column6: Zhè bān gōngchē de zhōngdiǎnzhàn shì huǒchēzhàn.
column7: This bus ends at the train station.

column3: A colloquial word for lunch, as in 吃中飯; 午飯 and 午餐 are the common words everywhere.
column6: Zhōngfàn nǐ xiǎng chī shénme?
column7: What do you want for lunch?

column3: A group label seen in health advice, news and ads; two ages share one ending (中年 and 老年 give 中老年), as in 青少年.
column4: 这种运动很适合中老年人。
column5: 這種運動很適合中老年人。
column6: Zhè zhǒng yùndòng hěn shìhé zhōnglǎoniánrén.
column7: This kind of exercise suits middle-aged and older people.

column3: The sound symbols (ㄅㄆㄇㄈ) that children in Taiwan learn before characters; the mainland uses Pinyin instead. Children's books there often print them beside the characters. 音 is 言 (“speech”) with one extra short stroke added inside its 口 (“mouth”).
column4: 小朋友的书上都有注音。
column5: 小朋友的書上都有注音。
column6: Xiǎopéngyǒu de shū shang dōu yǒu zhùyīn.
column7: Children's books all have phonetic symbols.

column3: A formal, written word for putting equipment into a building or place, such as lights, cameras or air conditioning. In speech, 裝 alone is more usual.
column4: 公司在大门口装设了监视器。
column5: 公司在大門口裝設了監視器。
column6: Gōngsī zài dàménkǒu zhuāngshè le jiānshìqì.
column7: The company installed security cameras at the main entrance.

column3: Color words usually end in 色, like 紅色 and 藍色. Before a noun they take 的: 紫色的花 is "purple flowers".
column6: Tā chuānzhe zǐsè de qúnzi.
column7: She is wearing a purple skirt.

column3: A set phrase for a household, farm, village or country that makes what it needs and buys little from outside. It is common when talking about growing your own food.
column4: 他们在山上种菜养鸡，自给自足。
column5: 他們在山上種菜養雞，自給自足。
column6: Tāmen zài shān shàng zhòng cài yǎng jī, zìjǐzìzú.
column7: They grow vegetables and raise chickens up in the hills, and live off their own produce.
